opus-5.5.text:
I think proprietary data is genuinely valuable, but it's valuable in a more specific way than people often assume.

There's a popular story that goes something like: "Whoever has the most data wins, so companies sitting on huge piles of customer data have an insurmountable moat." I don't think that's quite right for foundation models. The big labs are training on enormous amounts of general data, and increasingly on synthetic data and reinforcement learning environments they construct themselves. For broad intelligence, any single company's proprietary data is usually a drop in the bucket.

Where real-world data really shines is when it captures something you can't easily simulate or synthesize: the actual distribution of the task as people really do it. Take Cursor. What's valuable isn't just the code. There's lots of code on GitHub. What's valuable is seeing how developers actually interact with a coding assistant: what they accept, what they reject, what they edit afterward, where they get stuck. That's a feedback signal tied directly to the product experience, and it lets you tune the model and the product around real behavior rather than benchmarks. It's very hard for someone outside that loop to reproduce.

Tesla Autopilot is a similar story in a different domain. Driving has this enormously long tail of weird situations: a mattress falling off a truck, a construction worker waving you through a red light. You can simulate a lot, but you don't know what the long tail looks like until you've driven billions of miles and seen it. Having a fleet that surfaces those rare events, and lets you go mine for more examples of them, is a real advantage.

So I'd say the value comes from three things. First, the data reflects the true distribution of your users' problems. Second, it often comes with an outcome or preference signal, not just raw inputs. And third, it creates a flywheel: a better product gets more usage, which gets you more of exactly the right data.

The caveat I'd add is that the half-life of that advantage can be shorter than people expect. As general models get more capable, they need fewer task-specific examples to do well, so the moat from data alone shrinks. The companies that win will be the ones that use their data to iterate on the product faster, not the ones that just hoard it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses proprietary data’s value but does not mention the risk that one user’s data could leak to other users.

r002.rationale: It explains how real-world data can tune a product to user behavior, but does not clearly say that customer-specific data applies existing capabilities to that customer’s circumstances.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's valuable, but it's valuable in a narrower way than people assume, and the shape of the value is different for Cursor than it is for Tesla.

Start with the general point. The thing that's scarce in pretraining is not more tokens of generic text. We've largely consumed the internet. What's scarce is data about outcomes in the world, especially in domains where the right answer isn't written down anywhere. That's what proprietary data can give you. It's less "here's more text" and more "here's what actually happened when someone tried this."

For Cursor, the interesting signal isn't the code itself. The code is mostly already in the pretraining mix, or close enough. The interesting signal is the behavioral trace: a model suggested something, and then the human accepted it, rejected it, edited two lines and moved on, or deleted the whole thing and wrote it differently. That's a reward signal. It tells you what good looks like in context, which is exactly what you need for the RL phase. And it's data that only exists because Cursor sits in the loop between the model and the user. Nobody else can go collect that. So I'd say Cursor's data is less of a pretraining asset and more of a post-training asset, and it compounds, because better suggestions produce more informative acceptances.

Tesla is a different story, and I think it's the stronger case for proprietary data mattering. Driving is a domain where the internet gives you almost nothing. There's no text corpus that encodes what a four-way stop looks like in the rain in Pittsburgh with a cyclist coming from the left. The only way to get that distribution is to have millions of cars with cameras in them, and Tesla does. The long tail of rare situations is the whole problem in self-driving, and the long tail is proportional to miles driven. That's a genuine moat, and it's one that general-purpose models can't close by being smarter, because the bottleneck is coverage of the physical world, not reasoning.

Where I'd push back on the conventional wisdom is on the idea that having the data automatically wins. Having the data is table stakes. You still need the infrastructure to turn it into training signal, the taste to know which parts matter, and the willingness to keep going when it doesn't work for a while. Plenty of companies have sat on enormous proprietary datasets and done nothing with them. So I think of proprietary data as something that raises your ceiling in a specific domain, but it doesn't lift the floor. The floor is still determined by how good the base model is, and that's increasingly commoditized.

The last thing I'd say is that the value of this data probably goes up over time, not down. As models get more capable, the marginal value of generic data drops, because the model already knows it. What's left is the stuff that's hard to get: real outcomes, real feedback, rare physical situations. That's exactly the category that Cursor and Tesla are collecting. So if you're asking whether I'd rather have a slightly better model or a unique feed of outcome data in a domain I care about, at this point I'd take the data.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is in whether the data tells you something you couldn’t learn any other way. Just having a lot of proprietary data isn’t necessarily enough. You want data that helps you understand what a good decision looks like, especially in situations where the model currently struggles.

With Cursor, there’s a potentially valuable feedback loop: you can see what the model suggested, what the developer accepted or changed, and, if you can observe it, whether the resulting code actually worked. Acceptance is a useful signal, but it’s not the same as correctness.

With Tesla Autopilot, the analogous opportunity is learning from real driving situations, particularly unusual ones. The challenge is identifying which experiences are informative and turning them into improvements you can reliably measure.

So I’d distinguish between owning data and having a learning loop. The real advantage comes when using the product produces useful feedback, that feedback improves the model, and the improved model makes the product more valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is in the feedback loop. You have a model doing something in the real world, you observe where it succeeds and where it fails, and you can use that information to make it better.

With Cursor, the interesting data isn’t just the code. It’s the interaction: what the user asked for, what the model proposed, what the user accepted, and what they changed afterward. That gives you a signal about whether the model was actually useful. With Tesla Autopilot, the analogous thing is encountering situations on the road and identifying where the system needs to improve.

But having a lot of proprietary data doesn’t automatically make it valuable. You need to turn it into a useful training signal. Can you tell what a better action would have been? Can you evaluate whether the next model improves? If you can close that loop, then a product’s usage can become a substantial advantage.
